questions.subject: Government
questions.text: Government can be best defined as
options: a group of people living together in a defined territory
an association formed purely for economic gain
the machinery or agency through which the will of the state is formulated, expressed, and realised
a body responsible only for collecting taxes
questions.explanation: Government is the institution through which the state exercises authority, makes laws, and carries out its policies.

questions.subject: Government
questions.text: The ability to influence or control the behaviour of others, with or without their consent, is called
questions.explanation: Power is the raw capacity to make others act in a certain way, which may or may not be recognised as rightful.

questions.subject: Government
questions.text: The right or recognised power to command, enforce laws, and exact obedience is called
questions.explanation: Authority is power that is recognised as legitimate, typically backed by law, tradition, or consent of the governed.

questions.subject: Government
questions.text: The acceptance by the people that a government's exercise of power is right and proper is called
questions.explanation: Legitimacy refers to the popular acceptance of a government's authority as rightful, whether based on law, tradition, or consent.

questions.subject: Government
questions.text: The supreme, final, and unlimited power of a state to make and enforce laws within its territory, free from external control, is called
questions.explanation: Sovereignty is the highest authority a state possesses, both internally over its citizens and externally in relation to other states.

questions.subject: Government
questions.text: The aspect of sovereignty concerned with a state's supreme authority over all persons and groups within its territory is called
questions.explanation: Internal sovereignty means the state has the highest authority over all individuals, groups, and institutions within its own borders.

questions.subject: Government
questions.text: The aspect of sovereignty concerned with a state's independence and freedom from control by other states is called
questions.explanation: External sovereignty refers to a state's recognition as independent and free from the political control of any other state.

questions.subject: Government
questions.text: A politically organised community, permanently occupying a defined territory, with an independent government, is called a
questions.explanation: A state is a legal and political entity with a defined territory, population, government, and sovereignty.

questions.subject: Government
questions.text: A group of people sharing common history, culture, language, or ancestry, and a sense of unity, regardless of political boundaries, is called a
questions.explanation: A nation is defined by shared cultural or historical identity, which may or may not correspond to the boundaries of a single state.

questions.subject: Government
questions.text: A broad group of people living together, interacting, and sharing a common way of life is called a
questions.explanation: Society refers generally to people living together in an organised community, sharing customs and institutions.

questions.subject: Government
questions.text: Which of the following is a basic characteristic of government?
options: It cannot levy taxes on citizens
It is always formed by a single political party
It possesses the authority to make and enforce binding laws
It exists only in democratic states
questions.explanation: A defining feature of government, in any political system, is its authority to make, interpret, and enforce laws binding on the population.

questions.subject: Government
questions.text: An economic and political ideology advocating that the means of production should be owned and controlled by the state for the benefit of all is called
questions.explanation: Socialism holds that resources and production should be collectively or state-owned to reduce inequality and serve the common good.

questions.subject: Government
questions.text: An economic system based on private ownership of the means of production, free markets, and the pursuit of individual profit is called
questions.explanation: Capitalism emphasises private property, free enterprise, and market competition, with minimal state control of the economy.

questions.subject: Government
questions.text: An extreme, authoritarian, ultra-nationalist ideology emphasising the supremacy of the state and often a single dictatorial leader is called
questions.explanation: Fascism is a far-right, authoritarian ideology marked by dictatorial power, extreme nationalism, and suppression of opposition.

questions.subject: Government
questions.text: An ideology advocating a classless society in which all property is communally owned and wealth is distributed according to need is called
questions.explanation: Communism aims for a classless, stateless society where the means of production are owned in common and goods are shared according to need.

questions.subject: Government
questions.text: A traditional African social and economic system based on collective ownership of land and resources by the community is called
questions.explanation: Communalism reflects the traditional African practice where land and key resources belong to the community as a whole, not individuals.

questions.subject: Government
questions.text: A social and economic system, historically found in medieval Europe, based on land tenure in exchange for service or loyalty to a lord is called
questions.explanation: Feudalism structured society around lords granting land (fiefs) to vassals in return for military or other service, with peasants working the land.

questions.subject: Government
questions.text: A state that combines a market economy with extensive government provision of social services such as healthcare, education, and social security is called a
questions.explanation: A welfare state ensures citizens' basic well-being through government-funded social programmes, alongside a market-based economy.

questions.subject: Government
questions.text: Rights considered basic and inherent to every human being, such as the right to life, liberty, and freedom of expression, are called
questions.explanation: Fundamental human rights are entitlements assumed to belong to every person by virtue of being human, often guaranteed in a constitution.

questions.subject: Government
questions.text: The principle that no one, including the government, is above the law, and that all citizens are equal before the law, is called the
questions.explanation: The rule of law ensures that laws apply equally to everyone, government actions are bound by law, and no one is above legal accountability.

questions.subject: Government
questions.text: The organ of government responsible for making laws is the
questions.explanation: The legislature (e.g., parliament or national assembly) is primarily responsible for debating and enacting laws.

questions.subject: Government
questions.text: A legislature made up of only one chamber or house is called
questions.explanation: A unicameral legislature has a single legislative chamber, unlike a bicameral legislature which has two.

questions.subject: Government
questions.text: A legislature made up of two separate chambers or houses, such as a senate and a house of representatives, is called
questions.explanation: A bicameral legislature divides law-making power between two chambers, often to allow for more deliberation and representation.

questions.subject: Government
questions.text: The organ of government responsible for implementing and enforcing laws is the
questions.explanation: The executive carries out the day-to-day administration of government and enforces laws passed by the legislature.

questions.subject: Government
questions.text: Elected officials, such as the president and ministers, who form the political leadership of the executive, are collectively called the
questions.explanation: The political executive consists of elected or appointed officeholders who set policy direction, distinct from career civil servants.

questions.subject: Government
questions.text: Career officials who serve the government on a permanent, non-partisan basis regardless of which party is in power form the
questions.explanation: The permanent executive (civil service) provides continuity and administrative expertise, serving successive governments impartially.

questions.subject: Government
questions.text: The organ of government responsible for interpreting laws and administering justice is the
questions.explanation: The judiciary interprets and applies the law, resolving disputes and ensuring justice is administered fairly.

questions.subject: Government
questions.text: The power of the courts to examine and invalidate laws or executive actions that conflict with the constitution is called
questions.explanation: Judicial review allows courts to strike down legislation or government actions found to be unconstitutional.

questions.subject: Government
questions.text: The principle that the judiciary should be free from interference by the executive or legislature in performing its duties is called
questions.explanation: Judicial independence protects judges from political pressure, ensuring impartial administration of justice.

questions.subject: Government
questions.text: The theory that the three organs of government (legislature, executive, and judiciary) should be distinct and exercise separate functions is called the doctrine of
questions.explanation: The separation of powers theory, associated with Montesquieu, argues that dividing government functions among three organs prevents the concentration and abuse of power.

questions.subject: Government
questions.text: The philosopher most closely associated with developing the theory of separation of powers is
questions.explanation: Montesquieu, in his work 'The Spirit of the Laws', systematically developed the theory advocating separate legislative, executive, and judicial powers.

questions.subject: Government
questions.text: The system of mutual restraints in which each organ of government can limit the powers of the others is called
questions.explanation: Checks and balances allow each arm of government to monitor and restrain the actions of the others, preventing abuse of power.

questions.subject: Government
questions.text: Under a presidential system of government, the separation of powers is generally applied
options: strictly, with the executive and legislature elected separately and independently
loosely, with the executive drawn entirely from the legislature
not at all, since one person controls all three organs
only to the judiciary and not the other organs
questions.explanation: In a presidential system, the executive (president) is elected separately from the legislature, reflecting a stricter separation of powers.

questions.subject: Government
questions.text: Under a parliamentary system of government, executive power is generally
options: held by an unelected hereditary monarch alone
shared equally among three independent branches
fused with the legislature, as the executive is drawn from and answerable to parliament
questions.explanation: In a parliamentary system, the prime minister and cabinet are typically drawn from the legislature and remain accountable to it, reflecting a fusion of powers.

questions.subject: Government
questions.text: A constitution that is contained in a single formal document, deliberately drafted and adopted, is called a
questions.explanation: A written constitution is codified in one authoritative document, such as most modern national constitutions.

questions.subject: Government
questions.text: A constitution based mainly on customs, conventions, judicial decisions, and various historical documents, rather than a single formal text, is called an
questions.explanation: An unwritten constitution, such as that of the United Kingdom, derives from a combination of statutes, common law, and long-standing conventions.

questions.subject: Government
questions.text: A constitution that can be easily amended through the ordinary law-making process is called a
questions.explanation: A flexible constitution can be changed by the same simple procedure used for passing ordinary legislation.

questions.subject: Government
questions.text: A constitution that can only be amended through a special, more difficult procedure than ordinary law-making is called a
questions.explanation: A rigid constitution requires special procedures, such as a supermajority vote or referendum, to be amended, making changes more difficult.

questions.subject: Government
questions.text: A constitution under which the head of state is a hereditary monarch is called a
questions.explanation: A monarchical constitution establishes a hereditary ruler (king, queen, or emir) as the head of state, whether ceremonial or with real power.

questions.subject: Government
questions.text: A constitution under which the head of state is an elected person rather than a hereditary monarch is called a
questions.explanation: A republican constitution establishes that the head of state derives their position through election rather than heredity.

questions.subject: Government
questions.text: The process by which a bill passed by the legislature is formally signed and given legal effect by the head of state is called
questions.explanation: Assent is the final formal approval by the head of state that turns a passed bill into a law.

questions.subject: Government
questions.text: The stage of the legislative process in which a bill is formally introduced and its title read out, without debate, is called the
questions.explanation: The first reading is a purely formal introduction of a bill, with no debate on its content at that stage.

questions.subject: Government
questions.text: The stage of the legislative process in which the general principles of a bill are debated is called the
questions.explanation: The second reading is when members debate the overall merits and principles of a bill before it moves to detailed scrutiny.

questions.subject: Government
questions.text: The stage of the legislative process in which a bill is examined clause by clause, often by a smaller group of legislators, is called the
questions.explanation: At the committee stage, a bill is scrutinised in detail, clause by clause, and amendments may be proposed.

questions.subject: Government
questions.text: The final stage of the legislative process in a chamber, where the bill (as amended) is voted on in its complete form, is called the
questions.explanation: The third reading is the final vote on the bill as a whole, after all amendments from earlier stages have been incorporated.

questions.subject: Government
questions.text: A system of government in which all governmental powers are concentrated in a single, central authority is called a
questions.explanation: In a unitary system, the central government holds supreme authority, and any local governments exist only by its delegation.

questions.subject: Government
questions.text: A system of government in which powers are constitutionally divided between a central authority and constituent regional units (such as states or provinces) is called a
questions.explanation: In a federal system, both the central and regional (state/provincial) governments have constitutionally guaranteed powers over their own areas of jurisdiction.

questions.subject: Government
questions.text: A loose association of independent, sovereign states that agree to cooperate on limited matters while retaining their individual sovereignty is called a
questions.explanation: A confederation is a weaker union than a federation, in which member states remain sovereign and can typically withdraw from the arrangement.

questions.subject: Government
questions.text: One advantage of a federal system of government is that it
options: eliminates the need for a written constitution
concentrates all power in one central authority
allows regions with diverse interests to manage their own local affairs while remaining united
questions.explanation: Federalism accommodates diversity by letting constituent units handle local matters, while a central government manages issues of common concern.

questions.subject: Government
questions.text: One disadvantage of a federal system of government is that it
options: always leads to a single, all-powerful central government
eliminates the need for a legislature altogether
makes it impossible for regions to have their own laws
can be expensive to run, due to the duplication of government institutions at different levels
questions.explanation: Maintaining separate governmental structures at the federal and state/regional levels can be costly and lead to duplication of effort.

questions.subject: Government
questions.text: A form of government in which the head of state and head of government are combined in one person, elected separately from the legislature, is the
questions.explanation: In a presidential system, the president serves as both head of state and head of government, and is elected independently of the legislature.

questions.subject: Government
questions.text: A form of government in which the head of government (usually a prime minister) is drawn from and remains accountable to the legislature is the
questions.explanation: A parliamentary system fuses executive and legislative power, with the prime minister and cabinet accountable to parliament, which can remove them via a vote of no confidence.

questions.subject: Government
questions.text: A form of government in which absolute power is held by a single ruler or small group, without free elections or constitutional limits, is called a
questions.explanation: A dictatorship concentrates unchecked power in a single ruler or small clique, typically suppressing political opposition and civil liberties.

questions.subject: Government
questions.text: A government that comes to power and rules through the armed forces, often after overthrowing a civilian government, is called a
questions.explanation: Military rule occurs when armed forces personnel seize and exercise governmental power, typically suspending the constitution.

questions.subject: Government
questions.text: An organised group of people who share similar political views and seek to win elections and control government is called a
questions.explanation: Political parties organise around shared ideologies or interests, contesting elections to gain and exercise governmental power.

questions.subject: Government
questions.text: A political party system in which only one party is legally allowed to exist and contest elections is called a
questions.explanation: In a one-party system, a single party monopolises political power and no legal opposition parties are permitted.

questions.subject: Government
questions.text: A political party system in which two major parties dominate politics and realistically compete for power, as seen in the United States, is called a
questions.explanation: A two-party system features two dominant parties that alternate in and out of government, though minor parties may also exist.

questions.subject: Government
questions.text: A political party system in which several parties compete for power, often resulting in coalition governments, is called a
questions.explanation: A multi-party system allows numerous parties to contest elections and gain representation, often requiring coalitions to form a government.

questions.subject: Government
questions.text: The legal right of a citizen to vote in public elections is called
questions.explanation: Franchise, also called suffrage, is the constitutionally granted right to participate in elections by voting.

questions.subject: Government
questions.text: An electoral system in which the candidate with the most votes in a constituency wins, even without an absolute majority, is called
questions.explanation: First-past-the-post declares the candidate with the highest number of votes the winner, regardless of whether they secured over 50% of votes cast.

questions.subject: Government
questions.text: An electoral system in which seats in the legislature are allocated to parties in proportion to the total votes each party receives is called
questions.explanation: Proportional representation aims to match a party's share of legislative seats closely to its overall share of the popular vote.

questions.subject: Government
questions.text: A body established to independently organise, conduct, and supervise elections, free from control by the ruling party, is called an
questions.explanation: An independent electoral commission (such as INEC in Nigeria) is designed to conduct elections impartially, without interference from the party in power.

questions.subject: Government
questions.text: A body of permanent, professional, non-political officials who assist the government in implementing policies and administering the state is called the
questions.explanation: The civil service consists of career officials who serve the government of the day impartially, providing administrative continuity.

questions.subject: Government
questions.text: A key characteristic of the civil service is that its members are expected to be
options: members of the ruling political party only
politically neutral and impartial in carrying out their duties
questions.explanation: Civil servants are expected to serve any government in power impartially, without favouring a particular political party.

questions.subject: Government
questions.text: Autonomous bodies set up by government to manage specific commercial or public services, such as electricity or water supply, are called
questions.explanation: Public corporations are established to run specific essential services on behalf of the state, often on a semi-commercial basis.

questions.subject: Government
questions.text: One reason governments establish public corporations is to
options: guarantee maximum profit for private shareholders
eliminate the need for taxation entirely
provide essential services that may not be profitable enough to attract private investment
questions.explanation: Public corporations often run essential services (like utilities) that require heavy investment or serve the public interest, which private firms may be unwilling to provide.

questions.subject: Government
questions.text: The level of government closest to the people, responsible for local matters such as markets, primary healthcare, and refuse disposal, is called
questions.explanation: Local government administers grassroots affairs and services directly relevant to the immediate community.

questions.subject: Government
questions.text: One major source of finance for local governments is
options: statutory allocations from the central or state government
questions.explanation: Local governments commonly rely on allocations from higher tiers of government, in addition to internally generated revenue such as local rates and levies.

questions.subject: Government
questions.text: A major problem often affecting the autonomy of local governments is
options: the complete lack of any local government elections
an absence of any central government structure
too much independent revenue with no oversight
excessive control and interference by state or central governments
questions.explanation: Local government autonomy is often undermined when higher levels of government exert excessive financial or administrative control over local affairs.

questions.subject: Government
questions.text: A group that seeks to influence government policy in its favour without itself seeking to win elections or hold governmental power is called a
questions.explanation: Unlike political parties, pressure groups aim to influence policy on specific issues but do not contest elections to govern directly.

questions.subject: Government
questions.text: The centralised Hausa-Fulani political system, headed by an Emir with defined administrative structures, is generally described as the
questions.explanation: The Hausa-Fulani Emirate system was a highly centralised traditional government headed by an Emir, supported by a hierarchy of officials.

questions.subject: Government
questions.text: In the traditional Hausa-Fulani Emirate system, supreme political and religious authority within an emirate rested with the
questions.explanation: The Emir was the paramount ruler of an emirate, combining political leadership with significant religious authority under Islamic law.

questions.subject: Government
questions.text: The traditional Yoruba political system, headed by the Alaafin of Oyo and supported by the Oyo Mesi council, is best described as a
questions.explanation: The Alaafin's power was checked by the Oyo Mesi (a council of chiefs), making the traditional Yoruba system a form of constitutional monarchy rather than absolute rule.

questions.subject: Government
questions.text: In traditional Oyo Yoruba government, the council of chiefs that could check the Alaafin's power and, in extreme cases, compel him to abdicate was known as the
questions.explanation: The Oyo Mesi was a powerful council of kingmakers and chiefs that acted as a check on the Alaafin's authority, including the power to demand his abdication.

questions.subject: Government
questions.text: The traditional Igbo political system, generally lacking centralised kingship and instead based on village autonomy, is best described as
questions.explanation: Most traditional Igbo communities were organised as autonomous villages or groups of villages without an overarching centralised king, hence 'acephalous' (headless).

questions.subject: Government
questions.text: In the traditional Igbo political system, decisions were typically made through
options: a written constitution drafted by chiefs
a general assembly of adult males, councils of elders, and age-grades
a single hereditary king with absolute power
questions.explanation: Governance among the Igbo was largely democratic and decentralised, relying on assemblies, elders, age-grades, and title societies rather than a single ruler.

questions.subject: Government
questions.text: The British system of colonial administration that governed African colonies through existing traditional rulers and institutions is called
questions.explanation: Under Indirect Rule, the British used traditional chiefs and institutions as agents of colonial administration, rather than replacing them entirely.

questions.subject: Government
questions.text: Indirect Rule was introduced by the British partly because it was
options: more expensive than direct colonial administration
designed to abolish all traditional institutions immediately
cheaper and required fewer British administrative personnel
only applicable in areas without traditional rulers
questions.explanation: Indirect Rule reduced the cost and manpower needs of colonial administration by relying on existing local rulers to enforce British policies.

questions.subject: Government
questions.text: Indirect Rule was applied most successfully in Northern Nigeria mainly because
options: the region had no history of centralised government
the existing centralised Emirate system provided a ready-made structure of traditional authority
there were no traditional rulers in the North at all
the British preferred direct rule everywhere in Nigeria
questions.explanation: The centralised Hausa-Fulani Emirate system offered a hierarchy of rulers the British could work through, making Indirect Rule easier to apply there.

questions.subject: Government
questions.text: A major difficulty in applying Indirect Rule among the Igbo was that
options: their acephalous system lacked a centralised chief through whom the British could rule
Igbo communities had no council of elders at all
the British had no interest in administering Igbo areas
the Igbo had a strongly centralised monarchy similar to Oyo
questions.explanation: Since Igbo communities lacked centralised kingship, the British controversially imposed artificial 'Warrant Chiefs', which caused resentment and unrest.

questions.subject: Government
questions.text: The French colonial policy that aimed to turn Africans into French citizens by adopting French culture, language, and values is called
questions.explanation: Assimilation aimed to culturally transform Africans into French citizens, granting full French rights to those who adopted French civilisation.

questions.subject: Government
questions.text: The later French colonial policy that recognised African differences and cooperated with local institutions while still maintaining French control is called
questions.explanation: Association replaced Assimilation as French policy, acknowledging African cultural distinctiveness while retaining ultimate French authority.

questions.subject: Government
questions.text: A key difference between British and French colonial administration was that the British generally practised
options: no administration at all, while the French built full colonial governments
direct rule everywhere, while the French relied entirely on traditional chiefs
Indirect Rule through existing chiefs, while the French practised more centralised, direct administration
federalism, while the French practised confederation
questions.explanation: British colonial policy favoured governing through traditional rulers, whereas French colonial policy was more centralised and directly administered from Paris.

questions.subject: Government
questions.text: A major factor that fuelled the rise of nationalism in colonial West Africa was
options: the total lack of Western education in the colonies
the discriminatory treatment of educated Africans by colonial administrations
the complete absence of colonial taxation
the immediate grant of independence upon colonisation
questions.explanation: Educated Africans who faced racial discrimination and exclusion from top positions became key drivers of nationalist agitation for self-rule.

questions.subject: Government
questions.text: Which of the following was a common method used by early West African nationalists to press for independence?
options: Total boycott of all Western education
Refusal to engage with colonial authorities in any way
Immediate armed rebellion in every colony without exception
Formation of political parties, newspapers, and constitutional agitation
questions.explanation: Nationalists commonly organised political parties, used the press to mobilise opinion, and pursued constitutional means to demand self-government.

questions.subject: Government
questions.text: The Nigerian constitution that first introduced a form of regionalism, dividing the country into provinces with legislative councils, was the
questions.explanation: The Clifford Constitution of 1922 introduced the elective principle in Nigeria and established a legislative council with limited African representation.

questions.subject: Government
questions.text: The Nigerian constitution credited with formally introducing regionalism by dividing the country into the Northern, Western, and Eastern regions was the
questions.explanation: The Richards Constitution of 1946 divided Nigeria into three regions, each with its own legislative council, laying the groundwork for later federalism.

questions.subject: Government
questions.text: The Nigerian constitution that introduced greater regional autonomy and increased Nigerian participation in the central legislature was the
questions.explanation: The Macpherson Constitution of 1951 expanded regional self-government and increased African representation in central government institutions.

questions.subject: Government
questions.text: The Nigerian constitution that established a full federal system of government with regions enjoying self-government was the
questions.explanation: The Lyttelton Constitution of 1954 firmly established federalism in Nigeria, granting the regions considerable self-governing powers.

questions.subject: Government
questions.text: Nigeria attained political independence from British colonial rule in the year
questions.explanation: Nigeria became an independent nation on 1 October 1960, though it remained a monarchy under the British crown for a few more years.

questions.subject: Government
questions.text: Nigeria became a full republic, replacing the British monarch as head of state with a Nigerian president, in the year
questions.explanation: The 1963 Republican Constitution made Nigeria a republic, with an indigenous president as head of state instead of the British monarch.

questions.subject: Government
questions.text: The Nigerian constitution that introduced the American-style presidential system of government, replacing the parliamentary system, was the
questions.explanation: The 1979 Constitution shifted Nigeria from the parliamentary (Westminster) system to a presidential system modelled on that of the United States.

questions.subject: Government
questions.text: The most recent constitution currently in operation in Nigeria, which came into effect at the return to civilian rule, is the
questions.explanation: The 1999 Constitution ushered in the current Fourth Republic and remains Nigeria's operative constitution, though it has since been amended.

questions.subject: Government
questions.text: A country's foreign policy is best described as
options: the method used to select its judiciary
the set of principles and strategies guiding its relations with other states and international bodies
the internal rules governing its civil service
the process by which its local governments are financed
questions.explanation: Foreign policy encompasses a state's objectives, principles, and actions in its dealings with other nations and international organisations.

questions.subject: Government
questions.text: A key principle commonly guiding Nigeria's foreign policy is
options: Africa as the centrepiece of its foreign relations
permanent alliance with a single foreign superpower only
complete isolation from all other African countries
questions.explanation: Nigeria has traditionally emphasised African unity, decolonisation, and continental cooperation as central to its foreign policy.

questions.subject: Government
questions.text: The international organisation established after the Second World War to maintain global peace and security among member nations is the
options: Economic Community of West African States (ECOWAS)
questions.explanation: The UNO was formed in 1945 to promote international peace, security, and cooperation among sovereign states worldwide.

questions.subject: Government
questions.text: The organ of the United Nations with primary responsibility for the maintenance of international peace and security is the
questions.explanation: The UN Security Council, with its permanent and non-permanent members, holds primary responsibility for addressing threats to peace and authorising interventions.

questions.subject: Government
questions.text: The continental organisation that succeeded the Organisation of African Unity (OAU) in 2002, aimed at promoting African unity and development, is the
questions.explanation: The African Union replaced the OAU in 2002, with a broader mandate covering political and economic integration across the continent.

questions.subject: Government
questions.text: The regional organisation established in 1975 to promote economic integration and cooperation among West African states is the
options: Economic Community of West African States (ECOWAS)
questions.explanation: ECOWAS was founded in 1975 to foster economic cooperation, free movement of goods and people, and regional stability in West Africa.

questions.subject: Government
questions.text: The voluntary association of mostly former British colonies and dependencies, cooperating on trade, democracy, and development, is called the
questions.explanation: The Commonwealth of Nations links the United Kingdom and many of its former colonies in a voluntary association promoting shared values and cooperation.
